Slide styles for the Utrecht talk, second round

The first round had several of the habits that current design critics list as signs of AI-generated work. This round has three new styles, each built from something already in the book or the talk: the figures and their annotations, Michael’s corrgram, and the penguins themselves. A fourth, Contour v2, reworks the first-round Contour style without its tells. The first-round styles are kept at the bottom of the page, each with a list of the tells it shows.

Things this round avoids, from those lists:

  • small all-caps or letter-spaced labels above titles (“eyebrows”), and monospace labels used as decoration
  • strings of facts joined by dots, such as “Utrecht · 5 Nov · 2026”
  • cream paper with a serif and a rust accent, and near-black slides with one bright accent
  • italic or colored words in headlines, big stand-alone numbers, and boxes with a colored stripe down one side
  • centered layouts, hairline-rule “newspaper” styling, pill-shaped tags, gradient fades, and shapes that are only decoration
  • the same layout on every slide

Annotated figure

The figure is the slide. Titles are plain sentences that state what the figure shows, and notes sit next to the data they describe, linked by leader lines and colored like the species they name. The only other element is the slide number. The section divider is the talk outline with the current section in black, as a Beamer outline would show it.

Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, chosen for legibility at a distance; it was designed for low-vision readers.

Why it suits the talk. This is how people who work with data tend to present it: the plot carries the argument and the text answers “what am I looking at?” It also matches Michael’s own habit of annotating plots directly instead of using legends.

What to watch. Each callout has to be placed by hand on each figure, so it takes the most work per slide. Use callouts only where they help, perhaps 10 to 15 slides, and let the other figures stand alone with a sentence title.

In PowerPoint. Callouts are text boxes with straight connector lines. The outline divider is one layout, copied five times with a different line in bold. Atkinson Hyperlegible Next is a free Google font.

Corrgram

Built on the corrgram, which Michael introduced in 2002. Blue means positive correlation and red negative, as in his original. Ellipses are drawn above the diagonal and shaded cells below. Slides are laid out in square cells like the panels of a scatterplot matrix, and every corrgram on these slides is computed from the penguin data.

Every pair of measures separates the species

Each panel is an HE plot for one pair of variables, set out like a scatterplot matrix.

In every panel the H ellipse for species reaches well beyond the E ellipse for error.

52
Figure slide: the HE pairs plot, with the text colored to match its two kinds of ellipse.

Why it suits the talk. The corrgram is Michael’s own idea and sits halfway between the data and the ellipse, so it connects the opening sections to the multivariate ones. The square-cell layout borrows its structure from the scatterplot matrices and HE pairs plots that appear in the talk.

What to watch. The blue and red now carry meaning, so they should not be used for anything else; links and emphasis stay black. The threads matrix on the divider needs care to stay readable from the back of the room. If it is too small, keep only row and column 3.

In PowerPoint. Draw the corrgrams in R with corrgram::corrgram() or corrplot and paste them in as images. The threads matrix is a PowerPoint table with one cell shaded.

Field guide

The penguins are the talk’s recurring characters, so this style borrows from bird guides. Species have their Latin names and their plotting symbols (□ ● ▲). Section dividers are identification keys that lead to the right plot, and comparisons use a species table with real means. Italic is used only where a field guide would use it, for Latin names.

60
Figure slide: the answer to the table on the previous slide.

Why it suits the talk. It makes the penguins’ role as characters explicit, and keys are a useful way to show “which plot do I use when?”, which the audience will want to know. It also has the most personality of the three.

What to watch. The talk is not only about penguins. Galton, the coffee data and the school data need slides that work without species. The key and table layouts handle those cases; the specimen drawing should appear only on the title slide.

In PowerPoint. Keys and species tables are ordinary PowerPoint tables with dotted borders. The specimen ellipses are three ovals with transparent fill. Alegreya Sans is a free Google font.

Contour v2

The first-round Contour style without its AI habits. It keeps the first round’s palette, the penguin photo fading into the background, the contour lines on section dividers and the R code under each figure. Here is what changed:

  • Monospace is used only for real R code, and the code is copied from talks/R/.
  • There are no all-caps labels or dot-separated strings.
  • Headings are roman, not italic.
  • The stack of big numbers is now a figure slide.
  • The figures are redrawn in R on the slide background: axes and labels in the slide’s grays, and species in the “medium” penguin shades, which read better on dark than the “dark” ones.

On the divider, the section number sits at the centroid. The contours are labeled the way R’s contour() labels them, and the 68% contour is picked out in the light Chinstrap shade, because 0.68 is the level the book’s figures use.

Fira Sans for all text; Fira Mono only for R code

Start with one data ellipse per species

Each centre marks a species’ means. The size and tilt of each ellipse show its variances and correlation.

Pooling the three gives the E ellipse that the HE plot compares with the effect of species.

48

The MANOVA juicer

Four measurements go in and two dimensions come out.

The first canonical dimension (86.5%) separates Gentoo from the other two; the second (13.5%) separates Adelie from Chinstrap.

The arrows show how each measurement contributes.

peng.can <- candisc(peng.mlm, data = peng) plot(peng.can, ellipse = TRUE)
60
Figure slide with the layout reversed: text on the left, plot and code on the right.

Why it suits the talk. It keeps what worked in the first Contour style: a dark room, the ellipse as the recurring shape, and code that answers “how did you make that?”. Every color and label now has a job.

What to watch. Every figure in the deck would need redrawing with dark settings: par(bg = , fg = , col.axis = , col.lab = ) for base graphics, or a dark theme for ggplot2. Figures that can’t be redrawn, such as Galton’s diagram or the GIFs, would have to sit on a light panel. Some rooms show dark slides badly, so check the projector at Utrecht.

In PowerPoint. The contours are grouped ovals with their labels, saved as a picture and reused on each section divider with a different number. Code captions are text boxes in Fira Mono. Fira Sans and Fira Mono are free Google fonts.

First round: possibly AI-looking

These are the four styles from the first round, unchanged apart from a corrected penguin count. Under each is a list of the habits it shares with AI-generated designs.

Atlas Plate

A nod to the 19th-century statistical atlases that Michael writes about as a historian of data graphics. Figures are presented as numbered plates with captions, sections open like an atlas contents page, and slide numbers are folios. Galton's 1886 ellipse is the starting point.

Possible AI tells
  • Cream paper, a high-contrast serif and a rust-red accent: the “warm editorial” look that AI tools now default to
  • Small letter-spaced capitals above the titles (“A Romance in Many Dimensions”, “Part the First”)
  • Centered title and quotation slides
  • Double-rule frame and hairline rules: newspaper styling on content that isn’t a newspaper
  • Italic subtitles used as decoration

Flatland Shapes

The plotting symbols in the book's penguin figures (Adelie ■, Chinstrap ●, Gentoo ▲) become the graphic system. Each section gets a Flatland rank, from triangle up to circle as the talk gains dimensions, and a row of these shapes in the footer shows how far along the talk is. Flat colour only: no gradients or shadows.

Possible AI tells
  • Overlapping geometric shapes used as decoration
  • Big stand-alone numbers (“4 → 2”, “86.5%”) set out like a dashboard
  • One phrase picked out in a different color (“Hard to see.”)
  • All-caps tags in boxes, and an all-caps label in the footer

Running Head

The slides take after the printed book: a running head, a coloured spine, and section colours taken from the book's four part colours. Titles state the finding in a full sentence (the assertion–evidence style). In the footer a row of small ellipses marks the section, with the current one filled.

  • Running head and “Section” label in small letter-spaced capitals

Contour

A dark theme for a dim lecture room. The 50/68/95% contours of a data ellipse act as a map-like motif on dividers. Text accents use the light penguin shades, which are readable on dark backgrounds. Every figure has its R call as a caption, because the talk is about tools people can use.
